slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by locating the chapter inside the course: curves have already taught us to differentiate moving frames, and now the same habit is transferred to two-dimensional surfaces in three-space. The title visual should be read as a promise that every formula is attached to a point, a tangent plane, or an oriented surface piece. Emphasize that the lecture is not a catalog of definitions; it is a toolkit for deciding which measurements survive a change of patch.

slides.title: Lecture Route
slides.notes: Use this route slide to set expectations for a dense chapter. The first half of the lecture is local and computational: choose a patch, compute partial velocities, and build tangent data. The second half asks how those computations change under maps, how forms encode oriented measurement, and why topology forces us to compare many local descriptions at once.

slides.title: Regular Patches
slides.notes: Stress that a patch is not just a way to draw a surface; it is an instrument that reports coordinates and tangent directions. The cross product test is a compact way to detect whether the instrument is working at a point. If the two partial velocities become dependent, the apparent coordinate grid loses a dimension, and the calculus built on it no longer describes a surface there.

slides.title: Tangent Plane
slides.notes: Describe the tangent plane as the place where surface calculus happens. The ambient three-dimensional picture is helpful, but the vectors that matter are based at a point and spanned by the two coordinate velocities. The normal vector is useful because it separates tangential motion from extrinsic bending, but the chapter repeatedly returns to measurements made inside the tangent plane.

slides.title: Directional Derivatives
slides.notes: The curve definition prevents a common mistake: a derivative on a surface is not a free-floating arrow in space. A tangent vector acts on functions by asking how the function changes along any surface curve with that initial velocity. The formula is independent of the particular curve once the base point and velocity are fixed, which is why tangent vectors can be treated as derivations.

slides.title: Tangent Fields
slides.notes: Vector fields are best introduced as an organized family of tangent vectors, one at each point under discussion. In a patch, the field has two coefficient functions because the patch provides a moving basis. On overlaps those coefficients transform, so students should not mistake the coordinate pair for the field itself. The visual reinforces that the base point changes with every arrow.

slides.title: First Fundamental Form
slides.notes: Frame the first fundamental form as the measurement ledger attached to a patch. The three coefficients are dot products of the moving basis vectors, so they remember how the coordinate grid is stretched and sheared. This is a key bridge in the chapter: it lets students compute lengths, angles, and areas from local data while understanding that the numbers describe tangent geometry, not just a drawing.

slides.title: Differential Forms
slides.notes: Introduce forms as measurement rules rather than as mysterious notation. A one-form measures a tangent direction, so it is naturally integrated along a curve. A two-form measures an ordered pair of tangent directions, so it is naturally integrated over a surface region. The orientation language matters because reversing the order of the inputs reverses the sign of the measurement.

slides.title: Surface Maps
slides.notes: Maps between surfaces are where the calculus becomes functorial. The differential sends tangent vectors from the source surface to the target surface, while pullback sends forms in the opposite direction. The opposite directions are not a trick: a measurement on the target can be evaluated on a source vector only after the vector has been pushed forward by the differential.

slides.title: Area Integration
slides.notes: This slide turns the cross product from a regularity test into an area density. The parameter rectangle does not usually preserve area when it is bent and stretched onto the surface, so the factor measuring the parallelogram spanned by the partial velocities must be included. Orientation enters when the integrand is a two-form rather than a scalar density, because reversing the patch order changes the sign.

slides.title: Boundary Calculus
slides.notes: Present the boundary theorem as a unifying pattern rather than as a memorized equation. The boundary integral measures a one-dimensional accumulation around the edge, while the exterior derivative measures the corresponding two-dimensional density inside. Orientation is the bookkeeping that makes the two sides agree. Many computational mistakes in this chapter are sign mistakes, so the normal and induced boundary direction should be named explicitly.

slides.title: Coordinate Changes
slides.notes: This slide is the checkpoint that prevents the chapter from becoming patch-dependent algebra. Students should see two grids on the same surface and ask what has changed and what has not. Components, Jacobians, and coordinate expressions change; tangent vectors, form evaluations, lengths, and integrals are the geometric targets that must be preserved under the correct transformation rules.

slides.title: Orientability
slides.notes: Orientability is a good example of why the chapter cannot stop at local patches. Every regular patch provides a normal direction locally, but a surface may still refuse a continuous global choice. The lecturer should connect this directly to integration of two-forms: global signed area requires a coherent orientation, while local formulas alone cannot guarantee that coherence.

slides.title: Topology
slides.notes: Keep the topology discussion tied to calculus rather than treating it as a separate epilogue. Locally, a small patch can look like a disk and every formula may behave exactly as expected. Globally, a loop around a handle can measure information that no single coordinate chart sees. This is the reason periods, orientation, and atlas compatibility belong in the same chapter as derivatives and integrals.

slides.title: Manifold View
slides.notes: Use the manifold slide to explain why O'Neill spends time translating surface ideas into a broader language. A surface in three-space gives concrete pictures of charts, tangent vectors, and forms, but the definitions are designed to survive without the ambient space. This prepares students for later geometry where the object may be known through charts and transition maps rather than through a single embedding.

slides.title: Worked Ledger
slides.notes: This slide is meant to slow students down before examples or problem work. Most errors in surface calculus happen because one line of the ledger is skipped: the patch is not regular, the tangent basis is not tracked, the area factor is omitted, or the sign convention is implicit. Encourage students to annotate calculations with the geometric object being computed and with the check that would reveal a coordinate mistake.

slides.title: Exit Problems
slides.notes: Close with problems that ask for explanations, not just computations. The patch check tests whether students understand regularity as an assumption that can fail on a subset. The form check tests coordinate independence in a small setting. The integral check forces the orientation convention into the open, which is exactly where it should be before students proceed to later curvature and global geometry.

slides.title: Summary
slides.notes: End by naming the durable habits students should carry forward. When a surface problem appears, they should first choose a reliable patch or explain why several patches are needed. Then they should separate tangent data, metric data, form data, and orientation data before integrating or changing coordinates. The next chapters can build curvature and deeper geometry on this foundation because the measurement language is now stable.
